4. **16 CFR 455.1 carves specific sellers and vehicles out of "dealer" and "used vehicle."** Excluded are "a bank or financial institution, a business selling a used vehicle to an employee of that business, or a lessor selling a leased vehicle by or to that vehicle's lessee or to an employee of the lessee"; and "used vehicle" excludes "any vehicle sold only for scrap or parts (title documents surrendered to the State and a salvage certificate issued)." ([law.cornell.edu](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/16/455.1)) Employee-purchase and lessee-buyout channels — often genuinely low-cost — si

This report explains *how* a "low-cost alternative channel" produces a lower acquisition price than a franchised or independent retail dealership, what its component parts are, what holds true across every instance of the pattern, and where the pattern breaks down.

1. **No independent measurement of the private-party-to-retail spread.** Every quantified figure found (46%, 15%, "15–25% more than trade-in") originates from auction brokers, dealer groups, or car-shopping sites with a commercial stake in the comparison, and each rests on single-vehicle anecdotes. Cox Automotive publishes the wholesale index and a retail listing average (C7, C8) but not a private-party series. **This is the largest evidentiary hole in the concept**, and it sits directly under its central claim. 2. **Salvage-auction public-access state lists conflict in their details.** Second

**C1. Consumer-open auction channels recover margin through buyer fees that scale with the bid, so the realised discount is smaller than the hammer price implies.** Copart's public (non-licensed) buyers pay a tiered buyer fee reported to run from roughly $59 on bids under $500 to $549 and up on bids over $8,000, plus a virtual-bid fee of about $99 per vehicle for online bidding, on top of an annual membership of about $59 (Basic) or $259 (Premier). (https://feecalculator.pro/copart-buyer-fees/) These are third-party fee-tracker figures, not Copart's own published schedule; treat the magnitudes

**D4. The same Rule carves out further exemptions that remove disclosure from several low-cost channels.** Exempt actors include banks and financial institutions, businesses selling to their own employees, and lessors selling to lessees; Maine and Wisconsin are exempt because their state regimes are comparable. (https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/dealers-guide-used-car-rule)

This report covers the channels through which a retail buyer acquires a used vehicle **outside the conventional franchised or independent dealership forecourt transaction**, where the stated appeal of the channel is a lower acquisition price. In scope: government surplus and seized-property auctions, public and dealer-only wholesale auto auctions, salvage/insurance auctions, private-party (peer-to-peer) sales and the online marketplaces that carry them, rental-fleet direct sales, and buy-here-pay-here lots as a distinct low-entry channel. The report traces when each channel appeared, what lega

24. **The same mechanism is documented online.** Lewis (2011) found that on eBay Motors, online disclosures are significant price determinants and that disclosure *costs* drive both the level of disclosure and prices. ([*American Economic Review* 101(4): 1535–46](https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257%2Faer.101.4.1535); [full text PDF](http://recherche.enac.fr/~steve.lawford/teaching_papers/reading/lewis11.pdf)) Cheaper-to-disclose channels are systematically better-priced for good cars — which implies the cheapest listings cluster where disclosure is costly or absent.

33. The channel history runs in four phases: (a) 1945–1949, the parallel birth of the private wholesale auction and the statutory federal surplus auction; (b) 1947–1977, closure of wholesale to consumers and the first legitimate retail workarounds (rental-fleet direct sale, 1962 and 1977); (c) 1982–2000, institutionalization and then digitization of salvage (Copart 1982, online mid-1990s) and of peer-to-peer (eBay Motors 2000), with Manheim putting dealers online in 1996–1997 and Simulcast in 2002; (d) 2000–present, consumer-facing online retail and marketplaces absorbing the "alternative" lab

- **§1 spine** — the concept reduced to one exchange: a low-cost channel is a position on a price ladder where the buyer has agreed to perform, absorb, or forgo something retail pays for. - **§2 — ~95 atomic claims** in eight groups (price formation, taxonomy/access, fee stack, legal risk allocation, information infrastructure, history, failure modes, invariants). Each tagged with report+claim provenance (`[M-A1]`, `[H-7]`, `[E-23]`, `[P-C10]`), a confidence tier, and its URL. - **§3 — 18 contradictions preserved side by side**, none resolved away, each with what would actually settle it. - **

The organizing question is not "do these channels have a lower sticker price" but **"under what conditions does the channel's price advantage survive contact with fees, legal exposure, information asymmetry, and repair risk — and where does it not."**

5. **"As is" is not uniformly available, so the same channel carries different risk in different states.** The FTC guide: "If state law allows it, and you choose not to offer a warranty… you must use the 'As Is' version," and "In some states, use of the 'As Is-No Dealer Warranty' Buyers Guide may be legally sufficient to eliminate implied warranties. In other states 'as is' sales are allowed only if specific action is taken or certain language is used." ([ftc.gov](https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/dealers-guide-used-car-rule)) Any general claim about "as-is risk" in these channel

25. **Online-only retailers are a convenience channel, not a discount channel, and have a documented title-delivery failure mode.** Connecticut's Attorney General settled with Carvana for **$1.5 million** ($1 million restitution fund, $500,000 penalty with $250,000 suspended) after an investigation opened in January 2022 into hundreds of complaints involving "extended delays in title and registration documents, delayed payments to sellers, and deceptive representations of car conditions and features"; the settlement bars Carvana from selling in Connecticut "unless it provides valid title and r

27. **Government surplus is genuinely low-cost but has the tightest operational constraints.** GSA Auctions sells "as-is, where-is" with no warranties, no returns and no refunds "even if the item turns out to be defective"; inspection access varies by lot; payment is typically due within 2 business days and removal within about 10 business days; vehicles convey by title or SF-97. ([gsa.gov](https://www.gsa.gov/buy-through-us/government-property-for-sale-or-lease/office-of-personal-property-management/personal-property-management-for-federal-agencies/exchangesale-property/gsa-auctionssm-sales);

1. **Is adverse selection actually the dominant force in these channels?** Genesove (1993), the foundational study, tested whether dealer types that wholesale more of their trade-ins receive higher prices and found **weak** evidence for adverse selection. ([*Journal of Political Economy* 101(4): 644–65](https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/abs/10.1086/261891)) Peterson & Schneider (2014), decomposing the car into components, found adverse selection on transmission, engine and cold-month A/C, but **advantageous sorting** on vehicle body and warm-month A/C — concluding the net effect "may have

In scope: the channel as a mechanism — its price-formation logic, its access gate, its fee stack, and its risk-transfer structure. Channels treated as instances of the pattern: public (consumer-open) auctions, dealer-only wholesale auctions, salvage/insurance auctions, government surplus and forfeiture sales, and private-party sales.

**D1. "As is" is the defining legal term of these channels, and it is a transfer of repair liability, not a description of condition.** The FTC tells consumers that in an as-is sale "the dealer won't pay for any problems or needed repairs. You're assuming the risk of anything that goes wrong after the sale." (https://consumer.ftc.gov/articles/buying-used-car-dealer)

2. **Disconfirming source on the "wholesale channels are lemon markets" premise.** The standard justification for the wholesale discount is adverse selection — sellers dump their worst cars into the wholesale channel. Genesove's empirical test of exactly this, using dealer wholesale behaviour and prices collected at a wholesale auction, finds only *weak* evidence for adverse selection. (https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/abs/10.1086/261891; https://econpapers.repec.org/RePEc:ucp:jpolec:v:101:y:1993:i:4:p:644-65) This cuts against treating hidden-defect risk as the dominant explanation of th

21. **The headline opportunity is real and large.** J.D. Power's *Used Market Update* for October 2025 put the difference between wholesale and retail used-car prices at **$14,747 in September 2025**, versus "a bit more than $9,000" as recently as 2021. ([autoremarketing.com](https://www.autoremarketing.com/ar/analysis/the-growing-gap-between-retail-wholesale-used-car-prices/)) Any claim that alternative channels offer no arbitrage is refuted by this gap.

**C19. Buy-here-pay-here is an "alternative channel" that is cheap at entry and materially more expensive in total — it is the clearest disconfirming case for equating "alternative" with "low-cost."** A Federal Reserve FEDS Note published **2026-05-08** (Chyruk, Cox, Liu, Wang, Zoulalian) reports BHPH at approximately 2% of the $1.6 trillion auto loan market as of 2025:Q3 with balances up 214% since 2018; BHPH subprime APR of **25.39% vs 14.60%** at traditional subprime lenders and prime APR of **11.81% vs 5.65%**; a *smaller* average subprime loan size (**$15,402 vs $17,424**); **10% of BHPH

26. **Buy-here-pay-here is the clearest case of a "low barrier" channel that is a high-cost channel.** Federal Reserve FEDS Notes (2026-05-08, Chyruk, Cox, Liu, Wang, Zoulalian): BHPH dealers charge subprime borrowers an average **25.39%** versus **14.60%** at traditional subprime lenders, and prime borrowers **11.81%** versus **5.65%**; **10%** of BHPH balances were delinquent in 2025:Q3 versus **3.8%** for traditional auto lenders; BHPH loans are **16.63× more likely** to be in active repossession status (5% vs 0.5%); average subprime origination balance **$15,402**. ([federalreserve.gov](ht

This report covers **channels a retail buyer uses to acquire a vehicle *instead of* a conventional franchise or independent used-car dealership** because the channel is advertised or believed to be cheaper. In scope: public auto auctions, dealer/wholesale auctions reached through a broker, salvage and total-loss auctions (Copart/IAA), government and fleet surplus auctions (GSA), private-party and online-marketplace sales, online-only used-car retailers (Carvana and peers), and buy-here-pay-here lots. Out of scope and deliberately not researched: sibling frontier concepts, auction *mechanism de

**B2. The access gate is the primary partition of the space: consumer-open channels versus licence-gated ones.** Manheim, ADESA, and ACV require an active state dealer licence plus AuctionACCESS registration and auction membership to bid; individual non-licensed buyers have no direct route in. (https://www.jalopnik.com/2227796/how-to-get-licensed-to-bid-at-auto-auctions/) This is trade-press reporting rather than an auction-operator primary document; treat the specific registration steps as indicative.

**B4. Some channels split their own gate per lot rather than per venue.** Copart runs a "No License Required" inventory that a member with an ordinary account can bid on, while other lots require a business or dealer licence, and which lots those are is set by the state the buyer is in, not by Copart. (https://www.copart.com/content/us/en/landing-page/qp-no-license-required; https://www.copart.com/content/us/en/licensing/index)

**F4. Prices in these channels are not fully rational with respect to observable condition, which both creates and caps the arbitrage.** Analysis of 22 million wholesale auction transactions found large discontinuous price drops at 10,000-mile odometer thresholds — a car at 79,900 miles sold for about $200 more than a comparable car at 80,000 miles. (https://www.nber.org/papers/w17030) The same study concludes the bias is most consistent with partial inattention by *final retail customers* rather than by the wholesale bidders, which means the mispricing a channel buyer can exploit is not neces

- **The discount is real but structurally bounded for consumers.** The deepest-discount channel (dealer wholesale) is closed by licensing (C4), and the next deepest (salvage) is gated by state law and permanently taxed by title branding (C5, C15). What remains reliably open to a consumer — federal surplus, municipal impound, private party, rental fleet — is a narrower band than the headline "cars for pennies" framing implies. - **Fee regressivity inverts the intuition that cheap lots are the best value.** Because buyer fees are flat-tiered below ~$5,000 and percentage-based above it, the effec

**C12. The FTC Used Car Rule's protections attach to "dealers," and that status is defined by volume — which is exactly why the protections do not follow the buyer into most alternative channels.** 16 CFR 455.1(d) defines a dealer as "any person or business which sells or offers for sale a used vehicle after selling or offering for sale five (5) or more used vehicles in the previous twelve months," with carve-outs for banks, financial institutions, employee sales, and lessors selling to lessees. (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/16/455.1) Washington State's AG restates the same five-vehicl

28. **The private-party channel is contaminated by unlicensed dealers ("curbstoning"), which defeats the buyer's assumption that they are dealing with a prior owner.** State enforcement exists but is low-intensity: Texas DMV penalties for unlicensed-dealer curbstoning run from $1,000 per vehicle up to $4,000 per vehicle, and California enforcement commonly proceeds by investigator sting and citation. ([txdmv.gov disciplinary matrix](https://www.txdmv.gov/sites/default/files/body-files/Motor-Vehicle-Disciplinary-Matrix.pdf); [sandiego.gov](https://www.sandiego.gov/sites/default/files/legacy/cit

2. **The Rule's coverage flips on whether the auction is open to consumers — this is the decisive boundary for auction channels.** The FTC guide says "At public auctions, dealers and the auction company must comply," but "The Rule does not apply at auctions that are closed to consumers." ([ftc.gov](https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/dealers-guide-used-car-rule)) Consequence: the cheaper the auction channel (dealer-only wholesale, reached via a broker), the *less* federal disclosure protection attaches to the vehicle.

3. **Where the Buyers Guide does apply, it is contractually supreme — which makes its absence in exempt channels a substantive loss, not a paperwork loss.** The Guide's own text states: "Information on the window form overrides any contrary provisions in the contract of sale." ([ftc.gov](https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/dealers-guide-used-car-rule))

20. **Online private-party channels carry a distinct fraud mode — the vehicle that never existed.** FBI IC3 recorded approximately 26,967 fraudulent-vehicle-sale complaints with adjusted losses of $54,032,396 from May 2014 through December 2017, typically via a spoofed "buyer protection program" and prepaid gift-card payment. ([ic3.gov](https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2018/PSA180117)) Note this is an older reporting window; a current-period equivalent was not located in this run.

**A disconfirming source was actively sought and found** — claim 23 (Tadelis & Zettelmeyer) and claims 25–26 (Carvana pricing premium; Federal Reserve BHPH cost data) each cut against the concept's implicit premise that these channels are cheaper in total cost.

3. Tertiary sources report that Manheim's first sale in 1945 offered three cars and sold one **to a member of the general public**, and that the operation converted to a **dealer-only** enterprise in 1947. This is the founding event of the access asymmetry that every "alternative channel" later tries to arbitrage: the cheapest tier of the market was closed to consumers within two years of being opened. This 1947 date is attested only in tertiary sources and is **not** confirmed by Manheim's own published timeline — see Unresolved Disagreements. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manheim_Auctions)

11. The federal government today runs four distinct public vehicle-auction channels: GSA Fleet Vehicle Sales ("auctions of government-owned vehicles that are in good condition and ready to drive"), GSA Auctions (vehicles and other government-owned excess property), the U.S. Marshals Service (property "seized by Department of Justice agencies and other federal agencies"), and the U.S. Treasury (property "forfeited by owners for tax evasion or other violations of Treasury law"). (https://www.usa.gov/car-auctions)

24. **Disconfirming.** The private/direct channel is not welfare-superior even though it is nominally cheaper. Li, Murry, Tian and Zhou estimate a spatial search-and-bargaining model on used-car transactions and listings in a central-Ohio metro area (dated 2025-04-15) and find dealers "selectively trade more valuable cars, achieving substantial price premiums due to superior matching technology and bargaining power." Their counterfactuals show that "removing dealer advantages increases search frictions, distorts market allocation, and reduces welfare," and that weakening dealers "shifts trade

25. **Disconfirming.** The online-retail successor channels are not exempt from the same consumer-protection failures as the lots they displaced: in July 2024 the FTC took action against online used-car dealer Vroom for deceiving customers, failing to deliver on time, and failing to provide required disclosures. (https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2024/07/ftc-takes-action-against-online-used-car-dealer-vroom-deceiving-customers-failing-deliver-time)

26. Rental-fleet direct sale is the oldest surviving "no-haggle" alternative channel. Enterprise Car Sales dates to 1962 as a service of Enterprise Rent-A-Car founded by Jack C. Taylor, sells principally out of Enterprise's own rental fleet, and was an early adopter of haggle-free used-car pricing later used by CarMax and by online retailers such as Carvana. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enterprise_Car_Sales)

5. **Whether steering buyers to direct channels is welfare-improving.** The consumer-advice framing treats private-party purchase as strictly better on price. Li, Murry, Tian and Zhou (2025) find the opposite at the market level: weakening dealers "shifts trade toward less efficient direct channels" and reduces welfare (https://cowles.yale.edu/sites/default/files/2025-05/intermediaries-in-decentralized-markets.pdf). Individual saving and aggregate efficiency point in different directions here.

**A1. The same vehicle carries several published, structurally different prices, and the spread between them is the entire opportunity these channels exploit.** Kelley Blue Book publishes distinct values for the same car: Auction Value is "Kelley Blue Book's estimate of what a vehicle is expected to sell for at a wholesale auction"; Private Party Value is "the starting point for negotiation of a used-car sale between a private buyer and seller"; and Typical Listing Price is "representative of dealers' asking prices for a used car." (https://b2b.kbb.com/kbb-vehicle-values/definitions-of-our-val

**B5. Government surplus and forfeiture is a distinct channel family with its own operators.** USA.gov names four official federal channels: GSA Fleet Vehicle Sales, which auctions "government-owned vehicles that are in good condition and ready to drive"; GSA Auctions, for "vehicles and other types of government-owned excess property"; the U.S. Marshals Service, for "vehicles and other property seized by Department of Justice agencies and other federal agencies"; and the U.S. Treasury, for property "forfeited by owners for tax evasion or other violations of Treasury law." (https://www.usa.gov/

**B6. Government fleet sale is the one low-cost channel whose supply is not adversely selected on condition.** GSA Fleet vehicles are retired on a fleet-policy schedule and are described by USA.gov as "in good condition and ready to drive" (https://www.usa.gov/car-auctions), which is a materially different supply origin from salvage auctions (insurance total losses) or wholesale auctions (dealer trade-in rejects). Buyers still absorb the as-is/where-is term (D2).

**C3. Government channels shift the entire removal cost onto the buyer.** GSA's own guidance to selling agencies frames their duty as making it easy for bidders "to inspect and remove surplus personal property" — the removal is the buyer's job, not the government's. (https://www.gsa.gov/buy-through-us/government-property-for-sale-or-lease/office-of-personal-property-management/personal-property-management-for-federal-agencies/exchangesale-property/gsa-auctionssm-sales) Secondary guides state the corollary plainly: GSA Auctions ships nothing, and every lot is sold where-is with the buyer respon

**F2. Access looseness and disclosure protection move in opposite directions.** Dealer-only auctions exclude consumers and are exempt from the Used Car Rule (https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/dealers-guide-used-car-rule); private-party sale is maximally open and is also outside the Rule (same source, D3). Consumer-open auctions are the one point where a channel is both accessible and covered. The invariant is that no low-cost channel offers both retail-grade disclosure and retail-grade access.

This report covers **channels a buyer can use to acquire a vehicle outside the conventional franchise or independent dealer retail lot**, where the stated motivation is a lower acquisition price. In scope: public government surplus and fleet auctions, municipal impound and lien-sale auctions, salvage/total-loss auctions, dealer-only wholesale auctions (as an access boundary), private-party sales, rental-fleet direct retail, and buy-here-pay-here (as the counter-case of a channel that is cheap at entry and expensive in total).

**Met.** The report rests on more than three independent sources across distinct hosts, with a primary-source core: usa.gov, gsa.gov, law.cornell.edu (16 CFR 455.1), atg.wa.gov, federalreserve.gov, ic3.gov, dmv.ca.gov, mobilepd.org, longbeach.gov, vehiclehistory.bja.ojp.gov, and ftc.gov. A disconfirming source was actively sought and found — the Federal Reserve BHPH note (C19), which shows an alternative channel that is strictly *more* expensive in total, plus the title-branding and fee-stack evidence (C10, C15) that cuts against the headline discount.
